sections.h: The poor king, the pierced one and the struck shepherd in Zechariah 9-14
sections.b: Zechariah 9-14 has four figures that readers have joined to the Messiah. The king of 9:9 is righteous, rescued and poor, riding a donkey, and speaks peace to the nations. The shepherd of 11:4-14 is paid thirty shekels. The one 'they pierced' in 12:10 is mourned as an only son. The shepherd of 13:7 is struck by the sword. The Gospels use all four for Jesus (Matthew 21:5; 26:31; 27:9-10; John 19:37). Jewish tradition reads 9:9 of the Messiah and 12:10 of Messiah son of Joseph (Sukkah 52a). Whether the four are one figure, or the king is a figure of the prophet's time, is debated.

common: The king of Zechariah 9:9 is read as the Messiah in the Gospels and in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a).
uncommon: Some critical readers see chapters 9-14 as hopes for a Davidic king of the prophet's own time who did not appear.

sections.b: These chapters are built on the shepherd image. The people wander 'because they have no shepherd' (10:2); the LORD's anger burns at the shepherds (10:3); the prophet is made shepherd of a flock marked for slaughter (11:4-14); the LORD raises a foolish shepherd (11:15-17); and the LORD calls the sword on 'my shepherd, the man who stands next to me' (13:7). The base texts are Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 23:1-4. In the New Testament Jesus uses 13:7 of his own arrest (Matthew 26:31) and calls himself the good shepherd (John 10:11).

sections.b: Zechariah gives the book's two portraits of a king: the poor king on a donkey who removes chariots and horses and speaks peace to the nations (9:9-10), and the LORD himself, who 'will become king over the whole earth' on the day when he is one and his name is one (14:9). The nations that survive go up each year to bow down to 'the King, the LORD of Armies' (14:16). The two pictures join in the Gospels' entry into Jerusalem, where Jesus is welcomed as the king who comes in the Lord's name.

Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 quote Zechariah 9:9. The Hebrew has one donkey in two phrases; Matthew has two animals, Mark 11:2 and Luke 19:30 one colt, and John 12:14 a little donkey. The Gospels leave out 'righteous and rescued' and use 'gentle' (Matthew) for the Hebrew 'poor.' The Plain keeps the Hebrew words. The next verse of Zechariah, which removes chariots and horses and promises rule from sea to sea, is not quoted, and Christian readers differ on whether it is fulfilled now or awaits the second coming.

In Zechariah 12-13 the house of David is named beside Jerusalem in three promises: the LORD saves Judah's tents first so that David's house will not be proud (12:7), the weakest will be 'like David' and David's house 'like God, like the angel of the LORD' (12:8), and a spring is opened for David's house for sin and impurity (13:1). The spirit of favor and pleading is poured on David's house in 12:10. The clan of Nathan, David's son, is named among the mourners (12:12; compare Luke 3:31).

sections.h: Zechariah 14: a day for the LORD
sections.b: Zechariah 14 is the last and longest picture of the day of the LORD in the Twelve: the nations take Jerusalem, half the city goes into exile, the LORD fights, his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, light and darkness are changed, living water flows, and he becomes king over all the earth. Ordinary things become holy. It is the Jewish haftarah for the first day of Booths, and Christian readers divide on whether it is still to come.

The phrase 'on that day' (bayyom hahu') occurs about seventeen times in chapters 12-14, marking each scene as part of one coming day: the siege and rescue (12:3-9), the mourning (12:11), the spring (13:1-2), the shame of the prophets (13:4), and the LORD's appearing (14:4, 6, 8, 9, 13, 20, 21). The chapters join the Old Testament's language of the last days to a time of foreign siege, a king's return and the worship of the nations.

sections.h: Zechariah 14:4-5 and the return of Christ
sections.b: Christians have long linked Zechariah 14:4-5 to the return of Christ: the LORD's feet on the Mount of Olives (compare the two men's words in Acts 1:11-12), the holy ones with him (compare Jude 14), and the mourning of 12:10 (Revelation 1:7; Matthew 24:30). They differ on whether it describes the second coming literally, or the reign of Christ since his ascension (see the cards).

sections.h: The Feast of Booths in Zechariah 14
sections.b: Zechariah 14:16-19 is the only prophecy that names one festival as the test of the nations. The survivors go up each year to keep the Feast of Booths, and those who do not get no rain; Egypt, which has the Nile, gets a plague instead. The chapter is the haftarah for the first day of Booths. The festival's water ceremony (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9-10) lies behind the living water of 14:8 and Jesus' cry in John 7:37-38.

The oracle of Zechariah 9:1-8 names four Philistine cities, Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod, leaves out Gath, and ends with a remnant of the Philistines 'left over for our God' who will be like a clan chief in Judah. 'A mixed people' will settle in Ashdod. It is a rare prophecy in which the Philistines are included among God's people.

Zechariah 9:3-4 says Tyre built a fortress for herself, piled up silver like dust and gold like street mud, and will be struck 'in the sea' and eaten by fire. The wordplay, Tsor building matsor, makes the island city the type of proud wealth. Alexander took it after a siege of seven months in 332 BC.

Zechariah 9:13 sets 'your sons, Zion' against 'your sons, Greece' (Yavan), the only place in the prophets where Zion's sons fight the Greeks. Many scholars take it as a sign of a date after Alexander and as a reflection of the wars with the Seleucids; others read Greece as a distant western power known from the 8th century BC.

Zechariah names Egypt twice: the exiles come back from Egypt and Assyria (10:10), and the scepter of Egypt departs (10:11); in 14:18-19 the clan of Egypt, which does not need rain because of the Nile, is threatened with a plague if it does not come up to the Feast of Booths. Isaiah 19:19-25 pictures Egypt worshiping the LORD.

In Zechariah 10:2 the teraphim 'speak harm,' the diviners see lies, and dreamers tell worthless dreams, so the people wander like sheep. They are household images consulted for guidance (Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5; Ezekiel 21:21), removed by Josiah (2 Kings 23:24), and listed with divination in Hosea 3:4.

sections.h: The end of the false prophets in Zechariah 13:2-6
sections.b: Zechariah 13:2-6 pictures a land where idols, prophets and the spirit of uncleanness are cut off. A man who still prophesies is told by his own parents that he will not live, and they pierce him through. The prophets deny they are prophets, disown their hairy cloaks, and explain their wounds as an accident. The passage applies Deuteronomy 13 and 18:20 and echoes Amos 7:14.

Chapters 9-14 are two oracles (massa', 9:1 and 12:1), poetry and prose mixed, with no dates, no named prophet and no mention of the Temple builders of chapters 1-8. They treat prophecy in two ways: as the word of the LORD to the shepherd who acts out the sign (11:4-17), and as a danger to be cut off (13:2-6).

sections.h: The spirit poured out in Zechariah 12:10
sections.b: In Zechariah 12:10 the LORD pours out on David's house and Jerusalem 'a spirit of favor and pleading,' and they look to him, the one they pierced. The verb is that of Isaiah 44:3, Ezekiel 39:29 and Joel 2:28. Christians link it to Pentecost and to the Spirit who convicts of sin.

sections.h: The third that is refined, and the Philistine remnant
sections.b: Zechariah 13:8-9 says that two parts of the land will be cut off and a third will be brought through fire, refined like silver and tested like gold; then 'This is my people,' and 'The LORD is my God.' In 9:7 a remnant of the Philistines is 'left over for our God.' The remnant in these chapters is both the survivors of judgment and a people made new.

Three covenants appear: the blood of the covenant that frees the prisoners (9:11, from Exodus 24:8), the covenant with all the peoples that the prophet breaks when he cuts the staff Favor in two (11:10), and the covenant formula of 13:9, 'This is my people' and 'The LORD is my God,' which reverses Hosea 1:9.

sections.h: The LORD at war in Zechariah 9 and 14
sections.b: In 9:14 the LORD appears over his people, his arrow goes out like lightning, he blows the ram's horn and marches in the storm winds of the south. In 14:3 he goes out to fight the nations 'as when he fights on a day of battle.' Both draw on the oldest poems of the LORD coming from Sinai or Teman (Judges 5; Habakkuk 3).

Matthew 26:15 and 27:3-10 tell of the thirty silver coins paid to Judas, thrown into the sanctuary and used to buy the Potter's Field, and quote Zechariah 11:12-13 under the name of Jeremiah. Acts 1:18-19 tells the story of the field differently. The thirty shekels recall Exodus 21:32, the price of a slave killed by an ox.

John 19:34-37 sets the spear in Jesus' side beside the quotation 'They will look at the one they pierced' from Zechariah 12:10, and Revelation 1:7 joins the same verse to the coming on the clouds. The Hebrew reads 'they will look to me,' with the LORD as the speaker; the Septuagint reads 'because they mocked.' See the variants on 12:10.

sections.h: The two staffs and the shepherd's tools
sections.b: In Zechariah 11:4-17 the prophet plays a shepherd: he takes two staffs named Favor and Union and breaks them, is paid thirty shekels and throws them to the potter, and then takes the tools of a foolish shepherd. It is the longest sign act in the Twelve and one of the most puzzling; it reverses Ezekiel 37:15-22, where two sticks are made one.

sections.h: Zechariah 9-14 and the roots of apocalyptic
sections.b: Paul Hanson's The Dawn of Apocalyptic (1975) treated Zechariah 9-14 as an early stage of apocalyptic writing: a cosmic day of the LORD, a siege of Jerusalem by all the nations, light changed, water flowing from the city, and the LORD king over all the earth. The view is debated, since the chapters have no heavenly guide and no coded history.

sections.h: Like the angel of the LORD (Zechariah 12:8)
sections.b: Zechariah 12:8 says the house of David will be 'like God, like the angel of the LORD going before them,' the angel who led Israel from Egypt (Exodus 14:19; 23:20). It is one of the few places where David's house is likened to the angel.

sections.h: Hadad-rimmon and the mourning for Josiah
sections.b: Zechariah 12:11 compares the mourning for the pierced one to 'the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo.' Many take it as the national grief for Josiah, killed at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:22-25), as Jerome did; the Targum names Ahab and Josiah; some scholars read a mourning rite for a storm god.

Zechariah 9-10 promise that Ephraim will be restored with Judah: the chariot is cut off from Ephraim (9:10), Judah is the bow and Ephraim the arrow (9:13), the LORD saves the house of Joseph (10:6), and Ephraim becomes a warrior (10:7). Chapter 11 then breaks the brotherhood of Judah and Israel (11:14).

Zechariah speaks of the exile as a pit with no water that holds prisoners of hope (9:11-12), and as a sowing among the peoples, where far away they remember the LORD and return (10:9). The pit is the cistern of Joseph and Jeremiah (Genesis 37:24; Jeremiah 38:6).

Zechariah 14:5 remembers a flight from an earthquake 'in the days of Uzziah king of Judah,' the quake that Amos 1:1 uses to date his words. Josephus ties the quake to Uzziah's attempt to burn incense (Antiquities 9.10.4), a story not in the Bible.

Zechariah 14:9 says that on that day 'the LORD will be one, and his name will be one,' taking up the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) and looking to a world where all nations worship the one LORD. The verse ends the Aleinu prayer in Jewish services.

sections.h: The poor king and the poor of the flock
sections.b: The Hebrew word 'ani, 'poor, afflicted,' names the king of Zechariah 9:9 and 'the poor of the flock' in 11:7 and 11:11. Zephaniah 3:12 calls the people the LORD leaves 'afflicted and poor.' The Qumran Damascus Document calls its faithful 'the poor of the flock.'

sections.h: A spring for sin and impurity (Zechariah 13:1-2)
sections.b: Zechariah 13:1 promises a spring opened for sin and for impurity (niddah, the uncleanness of a woman at her monthly separation and of anything that kept a person from the sanctuary). 13:2 adds 'the spirit of uncleanness,' a phrase the Septuagint renders as the Gospels' 'unclean spirit.'

Zechariah 13:1 promises 'a spring opened for the house of David and the people living in Jerusalem, for sin and for impurity.' Ezekiel 36:25 pictures clean water sprinkled on the people. John 19:34 and Revelation 22:1 are the New Testament's water and blood and river.

sections.h: 'Holy to the LORD' on bells and pots (Zechariah 14:20-21)
sections.b: The inscription of the high priest's gold plate, 'Holy to the LORD' (Exodus 28:36), is on the bells of the horses in Zechariah 14:20, and every pot in Jerusalem and Judah is as holy as the bowls before the altar. Holiness spreads from the priest to everything.

sections.h: The Temple doors and the traders (Zechariah 11:1; 14:21)
sections.b: The Talmud reads 'Open your doors, Lebanon' (Zechariah 11:1) as the opening of the Temple doors before the destruction (Yoma 39b). Zechariah 14:21 ends with no 'Canaanite' (trader) in the house of the LORD; the Gospels' Temple scene (John 2:14-16; Mark 11:15-17) is read with it.

sections.h: The break between Judah and Israel (Zechariah 11:14)
sections.b: Zechariah 11:14 breaks the staff Union 'to break the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.' Proposals include the split of 1 Kings 12, the Persian-period quarrel with Samaria (Nehemiah 4 and 6), and the later Samaritan temple on Gerizim in Alexander's time (Josephus, Antiquities 11.8).

sections.h: The oracle against Hadrach and Philistia (Zechariah 9:1-8)
sections.b: Zechariah 9:1-8 is an oracle against the lands of the north and the coast, Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, Sidon and four Philistine cities, in order from north to south. It resembles Amos 1-2 and is read as Alexander's march in 333-332 BC, an Assyrian campaign, or a general pattern of judgment.

sections.h: Zechariah 9-14 in the Book of the Twelve
sections.b: Zechariah 9-14 holds two massa' oracles (9:1; 12:1), matched by Malachi 1:1, so many scholars read the last three units of the Twelve as one added block. Links: Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8 (water from the house of the LORD), Amos 9:11-12 and Zechariah 14:16 (the nations and the restored booth), Haggai 2:6-7 and Zechariah 14:14 (the nations' wealth).

In Zechariah 12:4 the LORD strikes the horses of the attacking nations with terror, their riders with madness, and the horses with blindness, the three curses of Deuteronomy 28:28 that were threatened against Israel. The covenant sanctions now fall on the enemies of the restored city.

In Zechariah 11 the prophet, as shepherd of a flock destined to be killed, asks for his wages and is given 'thirty shekels of silver.' The LORD tells him to throw it to the potter, and he throws it into the house of the LORD. The sum is the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32. The Hebrew has 'potter'; the Greek has 'furnace' and the Syriac 'treasury.'

The Mount of Olives is named in Zechariah 14:4 as the place where the LORD's feet will stand on the day of the LORD, when the mountain splits from east to west and leaves a very great valley for the people to flee through. It is the only place the Hebrew Bible calls it 'the mountain of the Olives.'

sections.h: The Feast of Booths in the age to come
sections.b: Zechariah 14:16-21 pictures the nations going up each year to keep the Feast of Booths, with sacrifices boiled in every pot. Dispensational and other premillennial readers see the millennial kingdom here; Reformed and amillennial readers read the feast and sacrifices as Old Testament language for the worship of the new age. See the card on Zechariah 14.

Zechariah 12:1 opens the second oracle with the LORD 'who stretches out the heavens, lays the base of the earth, and forms the spirit of a human being inside him.' The verb 'forms' (yatsar) is the potter's verb. The only place in the Bible where it is used of the spirit.

Zechariah 10:11 says the LORD will pass through the sea of trouble, strike the waves, and dry the depths of the Nile, a new Exodus for the exiles coming home from Egypt and Assyria. Isaiah 11:15-16 and 51:10 tell it the same way.

In Zechariah 12-14 Jerusalem is a bowl that makes the nations stagger, a stone too heavy to lift, the city whose people mourn, the place where a spring opens and living water flows to both seas, and the high place that stays in its place when the land is leveled. The nations that come against it come up to it to worship.
